airCheck.intro: Reads this phone's air pressure and compares it with the nearest US weather station's reading, worked out for the height of your position. Two sensors and a weather service in one answer.

airCheck.result.notAVerdict: A mismatch is not proof of anything. Weather moves, and a rough position moves the expected pressure with it.
airCheckMath.allowance.floorNote: Three uncertainties added in quadrature came out under the floor, so the floor is the allowance: a perfect fix is not asked for perfect agreement.
airCheckMath.allowance.note: Three uncertainties added in quadrature: how precisely your height is known, how little is known about the column's temperature, and the weather's own pressure uncertainty.
airCheckMath.answer.note: The residual is a distance, not a judgement: the same number is a match at one allowance and a mismatch at another.
airCheckMath.column.note: H is the height over which pressure falls to about a third. Warmer air is less dense, so a warm column is taller and pressure falls more slowly. Half the standard lapse rate stands for the column's mean rather than its surface.
airCheckMath.constants.note: Read from the SDK, not retyped here. The floor and ceiling are read out of the comparison itself, so they cannot drift from it. These are standard atmospheric approximations, not a calibration measured against a population.
airCheckMath.expected.note: Where the station's height is known, the reading is brought down to the station first and then to you, which keeps the station's own elevation visible instead of hidden inside one exponent.

continuity.anchor.header: What makes it the same phone
continuity.anchor.note: The sensors never prove sameness. This does: a key that exists in one phone's silicon and cannot be copied out, a signature over every reading, and a chain in which each reading commits to the ones before it.
continuity.answer.note: Compared with the pass before this one. A changed network or a sensor you turned off never breaks continuity; only the phone itself changing does.
continuity.coverage.note: Two fractions, kept apart on purpose. A sensor this phone lacks, or a permission you refused, makes a lane unavailable: it lowers how much could be said, never how much you are believed.
continuity.firstPass.note: Nothing has been saved from an earlier pass yet, so there is nothing to compare against. The next reading will have one.
continuity.forget.note: The saved fingerprint is the only judgement this app keeps between launches. Erase on the Settings tab clears the SDK's own stores.
continuity.lanes.note: What each one gave this time, and why not when it gave nothing.
continuity.network.note: The network is compared as a private code, never as its name, and a change is normal: it grades how much a change weighs, and never breaks continuity.
continuity.score.note: An estimate with its uncertainty, not a verdict. It needs both a history worth something and a live reading worth something: either one near zero pulls it down. A break throws the history away, and it has to be earned again.
continuity.unsigned: This reading carries no receipt, so nothing anchors it.
continuity.waiting: Waiting for a reading from the Sensors tab.
continuityMath.anchor.chain: Each reading is hashed and committed together with the root before it. Alter a past reading and every root after it stops matching; delete or insert one and the count and position no longer line up.
continuityMath.anchor.header: What proves it is the same phone
continuityMath.anchor.key: The private key is generated inside the phone and cannot be read out or copied, not even by this app. Only the public half travels. A new phone, a wipe or a reinstall means a new key, and a new key cannot claim the old one's history.
continuityMath.anchor.note: Three mechanisms, three questions. The key answers which phone, the chain answers whether the history was edited, and the sensors answer whether that phone was really present. Only the third is scored below; the first two are either true or the evidence is worthless.
continuityMath.anchor.sensors: A key can be exercised by anything holding the phone. The sensors are what say a phone was actually there, in real air, on a known network — cheap to read, expensive to fake for months.
continuityMath.break.note: Only the phone's own identity and its SIM can break continuity. The network is compared, but a change never breaks it: people move.
continuityMath.claim.gloss: A chain of readings from one phone. The break test says whether the chain snapped; the estimate says what the chain is worth.
continuityMath.claim.note: It is not a claim about a person. A phone taken from you carries its continuity with it, which is why this is one lane of evidence beside a document and a face, never the whole answer.
continuityMath.constants.note: Read from the SDK, not retyped here. They are chosen shapes rather than measured ones: the half-maturity point says when a history counts for half, not what a person is.
continuityMath.estimate.note: History and the live moment are combined the same soft way: both must be worth something. The lower bound is the tenth percentile of a Beta posterior with a weak sceptical prior, so few readings mean a wide gap and a low tightness.
continuityMath.fractions.header: 1. What read, and what could have
continuityMath.fractions.note: Breadth discounts how much this pass can claim. Coverage measures only the lanes that were able to speak, so an unavailable lane never counts as a silence held against you.
continuityMath.live.note: A geometric mean, so one weak part drags the result down and cannot be made up for by the others. The floor stops a single zero from wiping it out. Coherence is the only place a network change counts, and it is a nudge, not a verdict.
continuityMath.maturity.header: 3. How much history is behind it
continuityMath.maturity.note: Days count on a slow curve rather than a cliff, and readings saturate. Readings are weighted by breadth, so a hundred readings from one sensor never look like a hundred from twelve.
continuityMath.noBreak: No term was true, so continuity held.
continuityMath.states.header: Sensors, counted by what they gave
continuityMath.states.note: These add up to the numerators above, so the fractions can be checked by counting.

fusion.footer: Each of these says something no single sensor can, and shows the working behind it.
fusion.proofs.device: Which phone — a key inside this phone's Secure Enclave signs every reading, and a chain makes an edited history stop lining up.
fusion.proofs.note: Continuity is the middle one: it will say "same phone" about a stolen phone and be right, because it was never a claim about who is holding it. That claim is the third proof — and one key signs both, which is what lets the two be read as a single record.
fusion.proofs.person: Who the person is — Face ID, the passport chip, the licence, the face match. Signed by the same key, into the same chain, as everything else.
fusion.proofs.presence: Where it was — a position, how long it stayed, and the phone's own air pressure agreeing with the weather. Cheap to read once, expensive to fake for months.

glossary.appAttest.body: Apple's own statement that this is an unmodified build of this app, running on a genuine Apple device. It needs a one-time number from a server to answer fully; without one it reports that a challenge is required, which is a state and not a failure.
glossary.canonical.body: One exact way of writing the data down, so that signing and checking agree byte for byte: keys in alphabetical order, no stray spaces, times written one fixed way. Without it, two programs could describe the same reading differently and a perfectly good signature would appear broken.
glossary.chainRoot.body: The single value at the top of the chain, standing for every reading beneath it. Two people holding the same root agree about the entire history without comparing it reading by reading.
glossary.hash.body: A short fingerprint of some data, produced by a fixed recipe. The same data always gives the same fingerprint, any change gives a completely different one, and you cannot work backwards from the fingerprint to the data. Here it is SHA-256, and it is how a reading is summarised before being signed or chained.
glossary.merkle.body: A way of committing to a list so that it cannot be edited quietly. Each reading is hashed; pairs of hashes are hashed together, then pairs of those, up to one value called the root. Every new reading is added and a new root computed, and each reading records the root before it. Change, delete or insert anything and every root after it stops matching — so tampering is not merely detectable, it is visible at the exact position.
glossary.secureEnclave.body: A separate processor inside the iPhone with its own memory, built to hold keys. A key made there can be used — asked to sign something — but never read out, not by this app, not by iOS, not by anyone with the phone unlocked in their hand. That is what makes a signature evidence of a particular phone rather than of some software that knows a secret.
glossary.signature.body: Proof that a particular key approved a particular piece of data. The private half signs; the public half, which anyone may hold, checks. Unlike a password, checking it reveals nothing that would let you forge the next one. Here it is ECDSA on the P-256 curve, over a SHA-256 hash.

motion.footer: Lying still, movement and rotation stay near zero. Pick the phone up or turn it and they change.
overTime.break.is: A break is the phone changing underneath the key: a different device kind, or a SIM inserted or removed. The key survives, the chain keeps extending, and the earned history restarts from zero.
overTime.break.narrow: The test is deliberately narrow. A new network, a new city, a refused permission, an OS update: all normal life, none of them a break. A test that fired on those would be noise, and nobody would trust the times it did fire.
overTime.gap.how: A reading stays fully fresh for a day, then decays to nothing over the next two. Earned history stays where it is: it is the live half that fades, so an unused phone keeps its past and stops being able to say anything about its present.
overTime.gap.meaning: The live half falls to nothing after three days, but the earned half stays where it is, and the estimate is the geometric mean of the two — so it drops a long way and never reaches zero while a history exists. One reading restores it.
overTime.keyLoss.differs: This is the heavier of the two. A break restarts the count under the same identity; losing the key ends that identity. The old chain stays verifiable forever, but nothing new can ever be added to it, and the new key starts a chain of its own.
overTime.keyLoss.is: Losing the key is the other ending: a wipe, a restore to a new handset, or deleting the app. The key cannot be backed up or carried across, so the next run generates a new one.
overTime.reading.is: One reading is one pass over the sensors, signed and added to the chain. It takes about a second and a half, and it is the unit every count on these screens is made of.
overTime.reading.noSchedule: The SDK has no schedule of its own and never wakes the phone. How often to read is the app's decision, and the numbers below simply reflect whatever it decided.
overTime.reading.when: This app takes one whenever the Sensors tab is open, a few seconds apart, so a chain builds quickly here. A real app would take one when it is used, or once in the background, not continuously.
overTime.reset.note: Neither is a judgement about a person. Both are facts about a device, which is all continuity has ever claimed to be about.
overTime.timeline.header: What it is worth, as time passes
overTime.timeline.note: Computed with this phone's current reading quality held fixed, so only time and the count move. Days count on a slow curve with no cliff — half weight at 45 days — and readings saturate, so the first few matter far more than the hundredth.

threeProofs.check.attestation: Apple's own check of the app reports its state, and a challenge still outstanding is not a completed attestation. The two are kept apart on the continuity screen for that reason.
threeProofs.check.completeness: Whether the history you were handed is the whole history used to need a commitment published somewhere else. It no longer does: every reading carries the counter Apple keeps for this app's key, which the app cannot set or skip, so readings removed from a run leave a gap in the count that the run itself shows.
threeProofs.check.coverage: This app signs its sensor readings. Document capture and visits live in the Pulse app, and the position used for the Air check is not yet written into the evidence here. Shared mechanisms make the rest possible; what is actually signed is what can be claimed.
threeProofs.check.how: A signature establishes that the signed content was produced with the matching private key and has not changed since. A linked chain establishes the relationships and the ordering recorded inside the history you were given.
threeProofs.check.tamper: There is a button beside the export that alters a reading after it was signed. Use it, export again, and watch the check refuse that reading and name it. A check that never fails proves nothing.
threeProofs.check.time: Times here are the phone's own. Nothing on this screen establishes trusted wall-clock time, which needs a time source outside the device — so treat the order as proven and the clock as reported.
threeProofs.device.breaks: A wipe, a reinstall, a restore to a new handset, or deleting the app all destroy the key, because it is marked to this device and never included in a backup. The next run makes a new key, and a new key cannot claim the old one's history.
threeProofs.device.header: 1. Which phone, and its connection to your number
threeProofs.device.how: The phone generates a private signing key inside its Secure Enclave and the private key stays there. Signed evidence is checked with the matching public key, and each record commits to the history before it, so a verifier can check both the signatures and the order.
threeProofs.device.notProves: The device key identifies the signer. Receiving an SMS code does not prove which SIM or handset received it, or who was holding the phone.
threeProofs.device.proves: A persistent cryptographic identity for the device's evidence. A completed SMS code check records access to the number at that time. Available carrier and line checks provide separate context.
threeProofs.footer: Kept apart, each proof is honest about what it can carry. Signed into one chain by one key, together they say who, where, on which phone, and in what order — which is more than any of them claims alone, and exactly as much as the three of them can back.
threeProofs.person.header: 3. Who the person is, and recurring authentication
threeProofs.person.how: The passport's printed page and its NFC chip, with the issuer signature, the certificate's path to a government trust root and the hashes of the signed data groups reported separately from mere chip access. A driving licence checked field by field against the issuing jurisdiction's records. A live face compared with the document portrait, on the phone, with presentation-attack detection.
threeProofs.person.notProves: A matched field, an unmatched field and a field the issuer did not report keep their different meanings. Agreement elsewhere never turns an unmatched document into a matched one.
threeProofs.person.proves: A named human being, holding a genuine document, present at that moment. Face ID at every app open adds recurring authentication afterwards: the document-to-face check establishes who the person is, and Face ID re-authenticates them against the phone's enrolled biometric each time.
threeProofs.person.where: KenshikiCapture · CaptureSelfie · IdentityEvidenceApple (not shown in this app yet)
threeProofs.presence.absence: Missing permission, absent hardware and an unreported result stay visible as limits on the evidence. A result such as "not reported" remains exactly that, and is never converted into a confirmed absence of change.
threeProofs.presence.header: 2. Where it was, how it moved, what surrounded it
threeProofs.presence.how: Core Location supplies fixes and their accuracy; visits supply arrival, departure and duration. The surrounding radio environment — Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, cellular and connection context — recurs and ties to a place. The barometer's reading is checked against the pressure expected at that elevation, and the magnetometer's against the field NOAA's model predicts there.
threeProofs.presence.notProves: The constellation is assessed as a combination, not as independent location measurements: its sources have different precision and different dependencies. A place is not a person until the third proof is signed alongside it.
threeProofs.presence.proves: Repeated visits, nights and time spent somewhere build a pattern across time. A single fix and a recurring pattern carry different weight, and the evidence records when each observation happened and how accurately it placed the phone.
threeProofs.row: What each proof carries, and how they join
threeProofs.title: Three proofs
threeProofs.together.claim: A continuing, inspectable relationship between a verified person, their authenticated use of a phone, and the evidence that phone accumulates over time. The claim rests on the composition and on the history, not on any one proof.
threeProofs.together.how: One key signs it, and each record commits to the history before it, so the order is fixed and nothing can be inserted or re-dated afterwards.
threeProofs.together.limit: Continuous assurance means re-evaluating that relationship as new evidence arrives, and keeping the distinction between a directly verified event and continuity inferred from the record around it. The percentage is that component's estimate — not a probability that a named person is present, and not a NIST assurance level.
threeProofs.together.proves: The document and live face establish a named identity relationship. Carrier verification contributes phone verification. The device key identifies what signed the evidence. Face ID supplies recurring authentication. Visits, motion, overnight observations, the radio constellation, pressure and magnetism contribute continuing context.
threeProofs.together.today: In this app, only the first two are wired: the sensors are signed, the position is read for the Air check but not written into the evidence, and visits and document capture live in the Pulse app waiting to be brought across. The mechanism is the same for all of them, which is the point of showing it on the cheap ones first.
units.footer: Only how readings are shown. The SDK reports metres, kilopascals and Celsius whatever you pick, and the conversion happens where the number becomes words.
